h1: Keeping good brewers when bigger breweries come calling
title: Keeping Good Brewers When Rivals Call | Craft Beer School
desc: Why small breweries lose good brewers to bigger ones, what it costs and the pay, growth and ownership levers that actually keep them.
teaser: A bigger brewery can always offer more money. It cannot always offer what makes a good brewer stay.
standfirst: India's craft beer scene has more breweries than experienced brewers. A good head brewer at a small brewpub will get calls from bigger players. You cannot always outbid them, but you can make leaving a harder decision.
sections:
Money matters, but it is rarely the only reason. In consulting work we often see brewers leave because they feel stuck: the same four beers for two years, no budget for new ingredients, no say in the business and no path to a bigger role. A larger brewery offers more salary and also the chance to work on bigger kit, with a lab and a team.

Ask yourself honestly what your brewer gets from the job besides a salary. If the answer is "a lot of cleaning", the next phone call from a recruiter is a real risk.
Work out what losing them costs

Put a number on it before you decide how much to spend on keeping someone. Take a simple example with your own figures. Say finding and training a replacement takes three months. During that time your assistant runs the brewhouse, quality slips and one 1,000 litre batch gets dumped. If that beer costs you ₹120 a litre to make, the dumped batch alone is ₹1.2 lakh, before lost sales.

Add recruiting time, the founder's hours covering gaps and the risk of regulars noticing the flagship tastes different. Against that, a raise of ₹10,000 a month costs ₹1.2 lakh a year. The maths often favours keeping the brewer you have.
Pay fairly and review it on a schedule

You do not have to match a big brewery's salary. You do have to be in a fair range and show that pay moves. Review brewer pay once a year, on a known date, rather than only when someone threatens to leave. A raise given before the recruiter calls feels very different from a counter offer.

Consider a simple bonus tied to things the brewer controls: batches passing quality checks, beer loss under an agreed figure, a medal at a recognised competition. Keep it small and clear. Brewers trust numbers more than promises.

Creative freedom is the one thing small breweries can offer that large ones often cannot. Give your brewer a seasonal slot on the tap list, a modest ingredient budget for trials and real credit on the menu and on social media. A brewer whose name is on the board is less likely to leave it.

Let them collaborate with other breweries and enter competitions. Pay for a course or a conference each year. Learning keeps good people interested. It also brings new ideas back into your brewhouse, which helps the business as much as the brewer.
Build a path, not just a job

Show your brewer where the role could go. That might be head brewer over a second outlet, a seat in pricing and planning decisions or responsibility for training the next assistant. Write it down with rough milestones. Even if the path is slow, knowing it exists matters.

For a key brewer, consider a small profit share or equity, with proper legal advice. It changes the conversation from "my job" to "our brewery". Use a lawyer to structure it, because poorly drafted equity creates more problems than it solves.

Recipes and process notes are business assets. Keep them in a shared system the brewery owns, not only in the brewer's notebook. A confidentiality clause in the employment contract is sensible. Be realistic about non-compete clauses: Indian contract law generally does not enforce restrictions that stop someone working for a rival after they leave, so do not build your plan on one.

The best protection is documented process. If your flagship is written down well enough for a trained assistant to brew it, losing a brewer hurts less. Our guide to why breweries fail shows how often key person risk sits behind the problems.

Many brewers leave because the job is exhausting rather than unrewarding. Brew days that start at 6 am, cleaning that runs into the evening and weekend shifts covering the cellar add up. Look at the hours honestly. Can an assistant take over kegging and cleaning so the brewer focuses on brewing and quality? Can brew days be planned so nobody brews six days in a row before a festival?

Small kit improvements count for more than founders expect. A dissolved oxygen meter, a decent pH meter or a proper hop store tells a brewer you take quality seriously. A brewer who spends half the week fighting a leaking valve or a temperamental glycol chiller will happily move to a brewery where the kit works. Spending ₹50,000 on reliable kit can be cheaper than replacing the brewer.

Hold a proper conversation with your brewer twice a year about what they want next. Ask directly: what would make you leave? Most people answer honestly if they trust you. Some answers you can fix in a week, such as a new refractometer or a day off after a brew weekend.

Retention is part of a bigger skill: running a small team with clear roles, fair pay and the numbers to back decisions. That is hard to learn from a single guide.

Your first step: book a one to one with your head brewer this month and ask what their next two years should look like.
faqs: Why do brewers leave small breweries?
Pay is one reason, but brewers also leave when they feel stuck: no new beers, no budget, no say in decisions and no path to a bigger role.
Can a brewery stop a brewer joining a competitor?
Indian contract law generally does not enforce post-employment non-compete clauses. Confidentiality clauses and well documented recipes are more practical protection. Ask a lawyer for your case.
Is profit share worth offering a head brewer?
For a key brewer it can change how they see the business. Structure it with proper legal and tax advice.
